name: PT Golden Flower Tbk

frontmatter.title: A garment maker priced as a float artifact
frontmatter.summary: Golden Flower is a loss-making contract garment maker whose shares trade at a market value far above any defensible value for the business, its cash and its property. The premium is a function of an extremely small free float on a concentration-flagged stock, not of earnings. We initiate with Sell: the operating business earns nothing, its cash is payables-funded, and the regime is working against the float premium.
thesis: The operating business is a low-margin, make-to-order garment manufacturer with no pricing power; at the 2026 run-rate it earns a negative operating margin, and the last reported loss was driven by inventory and receivable write-downs on top of that.
Two customers, G III Apparel and Giordano Indonesia, took more than four fifths of FY2025 revenue, so the order book is a relationship with one US brand, not a market.
The balance sheet, not the income statement, holds the value — net cash, investment property at cost and an unfunded employee-benefit liability together carry almost all of the fundamental value.

The quoted price is a float phenomenon. Almost nine-tenths of the shares are held by two affiliated holders and the free float sits below the exchange's next compliance step, so a thin order book sets the marginal price.

The regime has turned — the name is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, is out of the IHSG, LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80, and faces a dated obligation to lift its free float; the FY2025 audit also reports two OJK compliance failures.
Our target is set by the house konglo lens, which keeps only part of the current premium over twelve months; the risk to a Sell is a renewed float squeeze, not an improvement in earnings.

catalysts.event: Deadline to lift the free float to the exchange's next minimum-float step
Effective date of removal of HSC names, POLU included, from the IHSG calculation; the HSC list also takes the name out of the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 at their reviews
MSCI consultation feedback deadline on moving Indonesia to Standalone; decision by 30 June 2027
FY2026 audited accounts and the AGM dividend decision

blocks.text: **SELL — target Rp4,000, -54.5% against the Rp8,800 price.** The target is not a call on the garment business worsening: it is the house konglo lens applied to a share price that has detached from the company. Our fundamental value today is Rp114 per share and Rp127 on a twelve-month basis — the second number is the first rolled forward at the cost of equity of 11.9% [S0]. The market pays Rp8,800, which is 77.3x the value today; on the twelve-month value the same price is a lower multiple, and either way it is a statement about the float, not about earnings. The lens keeps part of that premium for the probability that the float stays tight, and the probability-weighted twelve-month price is Rp4,000.

What the market is paying for is visible in the multiples rather than in the accounts. At IDR6,600.0bn of market value the company is valued at 60.5x its reported book value — and many times the revenue it books (IDR156.5bn in FY2025), on an enterprise-value-to-EBITDA figure that is arithmetically absurd because EBIT is negative [S0][S3]. Those are not earnings multiples; they are the arithmetic of a price set by a handful of shares changing hands — three-month average daily turnover is IDR321.4m [S0].

The business itself is a contract manufacturer of woven garments for export: it produced 1,133,616.0 pieces in FY2025 and employs 914 people [S3]. Gross profit was IDR20.4bn on that revenue and the reported operating result was IDR-17.0bn, but most of the loss came from IDR11.3bn of inventory write-downs and IDR4.5bn of receivable impairments booked in the same year [S3]. Strip those out and the company was still slightly loss-making at the operating line; the nine months of FY2026 show the same economics, which is why the base case holds them [S0]. A business that earns nothing is worth its assets, not a growth multiple.

Three things move the value from here. First, the exchange's free-float step due at the end of March: the public holds 11.4% against a next step of 12.5%, a gap of 1.1% that can only be closed by the controllers selling down or by new shares [konglo]. Second, the index regime: POLU is on the high-shareholding-concentration list, is out of the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026 and out of the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 at their reviews, with an MSCI Indonesia consultation that could move the country to Standalone by mid-2027 [konglo][konglo]. Third, the healthcare and property subsidiaries — a hospital in Semarang, a beauty clinic and land in Ungaran — which have so far consumed cash without producing disclosed revenue [S3][S4].

The pattern is familiar in Jakarta: a small, low-float industrial company whose share price multiplies
while its accounts barely change, then loses most of that gain when the index and the regulator turn
their attention to concentrated ownership. The fundamentals never move; the float does.

PT Golden Flower Tbk is a contract manufacturer of light and medium woven apparel: ladies' blouses, dresses, nightwear, men's dress and casual shirts, skirts and uniforms. Production is make-to-order — goods are cut and sewn after the customer's order, and the sales system follows order volume rather than a seasonal collection of the company's own design [S3]. The customer is an international brand or its sourcing agent, not the consumer; the company carries no brand of its own and no retail network.

**Mix.** Revenue in FY2025 was IDR156.5bn, of which ladies' blouses contributed IDR104.0bn and men's shirts most of the remainder, with uniforms and accessories reduced to a rounding error [S3]. The mix has shifted sharply: uniforms and accessories were a third of the business a year earlier and have all but disappeared, while the blouse line grew [S3]. That is a single-product, single-channel profile, and it explains both the thin gross margin and the concentration risk discussed in section two.

**Scale and footprint.** The company produced 1,133,616.0 garments in FY2025, up from 1,012,472.0 a year earlier, split between womenswear and menswear [S3]. It employed 914 people at the end of FY2025, most of them non-staff production workers, down from 1,080 in the data pack's headcount figure and consistent with a labour-intensive, low-automation plant [S3][S0]. Manufacturing sits in Ungaran, Central Java, with the corporate office in Jakarta; the subsidiaries are addressed to the same Ungaran site and to Semarang [S3].

**What else the company now owns.** The group is no longer only a garment maker. Wholly owned subsidiaries include a hospital in Semarang (PT Rumah Sakit Majapahit), a garment entity, two real estate companies holding land at Ungaran, and a trading company; a beauty-clinic business, PT Oracle Medika Indonesia, was established in 2024 with the company holding seventy per cent [S3][S4]. The group has also put IDR80.2bn of investment property on the balance sheet, of which IDR18.5bn was added in FY2025 and the rest carried over from earlier years [S3, note 10]. None of these businesses yet appears as a revenue line: the product note still shows only garments [S3]. The healthcare and property ventures are, for now, an allocation of capital rather than a source of earnings.

**Ownership and group.** Two affiliated holders own almost all of the shares: PT Profashion Apparel holds almost eighty per cent and PT Golden Flower Global Resources a further eight and a half, leaving public shareholders with 11.5% [S3]. The company is not part of one of the large family conglomerates in the house registry; it is flagged as a konglo name because of the concentration of its register and its place on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, not because of a group affiliation [konglo]. Management is professional rather than family: the president director and the finance director are long-serving executives and the board declares no affiliation with the controlling shareholders [S3].

**Strategy as stated.** The annual report frames the strategy around manufacturing excellence and penetrating global markets, with the garment business as the operating core and the new healthcare and property entities as diversification [S3]. There is no quantified plan — no revenue target, no capacity expansion figure, no clinic roll-out timetable — in the FY2025 report, which is itself a governance observation: the market has been asked to price a transformation the accounts do not describe.

Contract apparel manufacturing is a scale-and-cost game. The manufacturer is paid a conversion fee on
fabric the brand often nominates, so margins are thin, working capital is short and the customer holds
the pricing power. Value accrues to plants that run full and defect-free; a sub-scale plant with one
dominant buyer has almost no defence.

**Where the revenue comes from.** Golden Flower's sales are export-led. In FY2025 the United States took IDR86.1bn of revenue and Indonesia IDR56.6bn, with Hong Kong, Mexico, Canada, Korea, Panama and the Netherlands making up the rest [S3]. The American share is the single most important variable in the model: a change in the tariff treatment of Indonesian apparel moves the company's addressable order book more than any decision management can take.

**The tariff regime.** Under the reciprocal-tariff agreement the Indonesian industry obtained a zero rate only for cotton and its derivatives; finished apparel, which is what Golden Flower makes, is subject to a 19.0% tariff when it enters the United States [S6]. That asymmetry favours integrated mills and disadvantages cut-and-sew converters, and it is the reason the company's own annual report puts diversification into the domestic market and into non-apparel activities at the centre of its strategy [S3].

**Demand and growth.** Indonesia Eximbank Institute expects national textile exports to grow around 3.2% in 2026, and up to 4.0% in 2027, after a much weaker realised rate in the current year [S5]. The same source names Vietnam and China as the competitive pressure: both have larger scale, cheaper energy and, in Vietnam's case, a more favourable tariff position with the United States [S5]. For a sub-scale converter the industry growth rate is a ceiling, not a forecast.

**Policy support.** The government is preparing a new incentive package for export-oriented textile producers, still at the design stage as of November 2026 [S7], and the annual report cites labour intensity, fiscal incentives and the Making Indonesia road map as the policy backdrop [S3]. Support of this kind helps cash flow at the margin; it does not create pricing power.

**Cost and currency.** Costs are domestic: wages, fabric, utilities. The rupiah is the reporting currency and the macro deck has the dollar strengthening to 18,350 by FY2027E from 18,190 spot [S0]. A weaker rupiah helps an exporter's rupiah revenue but raises the cost of imported fabric and trim, so the net effect on a converter with thin margins is ambiguous — the company books foreign-exchange gains and losses below the operating line, and they have been material relative to operating profit [S3].

**Structure and competitive position.** The Indonesian apparel industry is fragmented: thousands of small cut-and-sew units, a handful of listed converters, and buyer power concentrated in a few global brands and their sourcing agents. Golden Flower is a challenger by any measure: revenue of IDR156.5bn and output of 1,133,616.0 pieces is a single plant's scale in a national industry [S3]. Buyer concentration is not a description here, it is a number: G III Apparel Group took IDR78.5bn of FY2025 revenue and Giordano Indonesia IDR53.7bn — four fifths of the group between them — and G III alone is almost the whole of the IDR86.1bn booked to the United States [S3, note 20c]. Management attributes the FY2025 volume increase to new customers [S3], which is the honest description of growth in this industry — it is won order by order, and it can be lost order by order. The bear case therefore shocks the revenue line directly: a cut of an eighth of the G III programme is about a sixteenth of group revenue, and that is a single commercial decision by one buyer.

**Five forces.** Buyer power is strong and rising, because brands multi-source and can move a program between countries in a season. Supplier power sits with fabric mills, which set the input price the converter passes through with a lag. The threat of new entrants is high: a sewing line is cheap, and Indonesia has surplus capacity after several years of import competition. Substitutes are a matter of fashion rather than technology. Rivalry is intense and price-based, with Vietnam and Bangladesh setting the reference cost [S5]. On that reading the industry earns, at best, its cost of capital in a good year, and a sub-scale participant earns less.

**Moat.** There is none that we can evidence. The company reports no long-term contracts, no proprietary product, no brand and no distribution network of its own; its assets are plant, land and a customer list. The one defensible asset is the Ungaran land and buildings carried as investment property [S3], which is a property play rather than an apparel moat.

Apparel sourcing migrates to wherever the total landed cost is lowest, and tariff engineering decides
which country that is. Converters live on the spread between the brand's price and the mill's price,
so scale, utilisation and defect rates are the whole game. That is why the sector's listed survivors
tend to be either very large or vertically integrated.

**The history is a flat line with two shocks in it.** Revenue went from IDR87.6bn in FY2023 to IDR135.5bn in FY2024 and IDR156.5bn in FY2025 — a recovery, not a growth trend [S3]. Volume explains almost all of it: output rose from 1,012,472.0 pieces to 1,133,616.0 on new orders, and the rupiah value per piece was broadly stable [S3]. Gross margin moved from 13.3% to 7.6% to 13.0%, which is the normal range for a converter buying fabric at spot and quoting orders months ahead [S3].

**What actually happened in FY2025.** The reported operating loss of IDR-17.0bn is not a demand story. Total SG&A of IDR37.3bn — of which IDR3.2bn was selling expense — contains IDR11.3bn of inventory write-downs and IDR4.5bn of trade-receivable impairment [S3]. Both are non-cash, both are operating in the accounts' own presentation, and both are the kind of charge that precedes a normalisation year or signals a problem with what is sitting in the warehouse and on the customer ledger. Excluding them, the company's operating result was close to nil on IDR156.5bn of revenue [S3].

**Restatement against the data pack.** Two lines in the pack are wrong and we have rebuilt the history from the audited accounts. First, D&A: the pack carries only the slice of depreciation allocated to G&A — about one twenty-second of the real charge — while the notes show total depreciation and amortisation of IDR3.4bn, split between cost of revenue and G&A [S3]; our restated line uses the audited total, so the pack figure and the modelled figure are not the same number. Second, EBIT and SG&A: the pack treats most of the write-downs as non-operating, so its EBIT is materially better and its SG&A materially lower than the accounts [S3]. Both are restated in the model (F5, F9, F31), and the effect is that FY2025 EBITDA is IDR-13.6bn, not the small negative the pack implies.

**The 2026 run-rate is the base, stated exactly.** Nine months of FY2026 were earned at the gross margin now shown as the FY2026E assumption, with EBIT essentially at zero on the pack's numbers [S0]. The last audited year's 13.0% is the outlier, not the anchor: FY2024 earned 7.6%, and the mix change the notes show is mens shirts replacing uniforms, while the blouse share barely moved [S3, note 20b]. There is no sourced reason to restore the FY2025 margin, so we do not.

**Costs and margin path.** We hold gross margin and SG&A at the 2026 nine-month run-rates through FY2030E: 9.5% and 10.0% of revenue [S0]. The FY2025 SG&A line of IDR37.3bn looked far higher only because it carried the write-downs; normalised it was still above the current run-rate. The result is an operating margin that stays at the last actual: EBIT is IDR-0.8bn in FY2026E and IDR-1.0bn by FY2030E, on revenue of IDR197.6bn. That is what a converter with no pricing power looks like when the last nine months are the anchor. Margin recovery is a bull-case shock, not the base — and the base is not a cautious case either, it is the arithmetic of the run-rate.

**Cash flow and the working-capital trick.** FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR32.3bn, against a net loss of IDR-13.1bn [S3]. That gap is not operating excellence. Trade payables rose from IDR6.7bn at end-2024 to IDR44.8bn at end-2025 [S3] and further again by 30 September 2026 [S0], so the company financed itself by paying suppliers later: cash from customers was stable while payments to suppliers and employees fell year on year [S3]. On the method card's accruals screen this is the flag that matters most — cash conversion looks superb and is entirely a balance-sheet stretch — and it is a liability that has to be refinanced or repaid. Our base case assumes the stretched payables persist, because that is the last actual position and the September 2026 balance sheet still shows negative working capital [S0]; the bear case assumes they normalise, which is why the bear scenario shocks the working-capital ratio rather than the volume.

**Capex and capital allocation.** Purchases of fixed assets were IDR3.6bn in FY2025; the investment-property outflow was IDR18.5bn, on top of the IDR80.2bn already carried, against operating cash flow of IDR32.3bn [S3]. The company pays no dividend and has never paid one [S3]. So the honest description is not that it spent its cash on property: it spent roughly what its operating cash flow generated, in a year when operating cash flow was itself payables-funded (see below), and it also added a hospital and a clinic. Capital is being redirected from a business that earns nothing into ventures that do not yet disclose revenue — defensible as an attempt to redeploy a cash pile, questionable as a use of a minority shareholder's capital when the controller holds almost nine-tenths of the shares.

**Balance sheet: the year-end accounts and the September position are two different things.** The audited FY2025 balance sheet held IDR76.7bn of cash against IDR44.0bn of debt — a net cash position — and that is the balance sheet the forecast year rolls forward from [S3]. The valuation does not use it. The DCF table below carries the net cash it actually capitalises, which is the 30 September 2026 position on the data pack: cash rose by about a third over the first nine months while debt was roughly flat, because nine months of operating cash flow were positive in a year with a reported loss [S0]. That cash build is the payables stretch again — trade payables reached IDR44.8bn at end-2025 and rose further by September — so the net cash the DCF adds is real, but it is funded by suppliers and it is the item the bear case removes. We do not restate the FY2025 fact to the September date: the pack is the only record of the interim balance sheet, the company's investor site carries no Q3 2026 statements, and the DCF table is the reconciliation between the two dates. The debt is short-term working-capital paper secured on machinery [S3]. The liability that does not appear in net debt is the unfunded employee-benefit obligation of IDR27.4bn, which is real, contractual and rising with severance rules; we treat it as debt-like in the valuation bridge [S3]. Equity of IDR111.7bn is flattered by an other-comprehensive-income balance that predates the periods presented in the accounts, against which sits an accumulated deficit [S3][S4] — book value is not a clean measure of asset backing here, which is why the valuation anchors on the asset side rather than on book value per share. One reading note on the financial summary: its FY2026E net-debt line is a forecast built forward from the FY2025 year-end and does not tie to the September position the DCF capitalises, so read that line as the year's cash flow, not as the balance sheet the valuation uses.

**Earnings-quality verdict.** Four optics-class flags, none manipulation-class. Payables-funded cash flow; write-downs booked in the year management would most like to reset the base; a market capitalisation with no earnings support; and two compliance failures the auditor reports in the FY2025 notes — a material transaction completed without an appraiser, disclosure, OJK filing or shareholder approval under POJK 17/2020, and affiliated transactions with the subsidiaries done without the POJK 42/2020 steps [S3, auditor's report]. Related-party exposure is small but not nil: no sales to or purchases from related parties, a small other receivable from a commonly controlled entity, and a land lease from PT Siliwangi Bimantara Perdana with a lease liability of IDR3.1bn at end-2025 [S3, note 27]. The auditor is a small local firm, and the accounts carry an unqualified opinion — but an unqualified opinion with a compliance finding in the same report is exactly the optics class the method card describes, not a clean bill of health. We would not treat the reported numbers as fabricated; we do treat them as a poor guide to value.

**Why this method set.** The industry card's default valuation is a DCF, and for once the default is the right tool for an unusual reason: there are no earnings to capitalise. The company has reported a loss in each of the last three years and earns a negative operating margin at the 2026 run-rate [S3], so a P/E is undefined — the engine drops it — and an EV/EBITDA is meaningless because EBITDA is a tiny fraction of the market value (2409.6x). What remains is a free-cash-flow model anchored on the balance sheet, cross-checked against the market's own book multiple for Indonesian apparel converters. The weights are not a conviction call: the industry default splits the value between DCF, P/E and P/BV, and with the P/E undefined the two remaining legs renormalise in proportion to 71.4% DCF and 28.6% P/BV, which is the arithmetic the engine applies.
**Cost of capital.**

The build is the house one: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, the Indonesian country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 (the industry default), and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% at a debt weight of 0.6%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.9% and a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent for rupiah names [S3]. The band is not the constraint here; the cash flows are.
**The DCF.**

The operating business is worth an enterprise value of IDR1.3bn. The terminal value is negative, and that is the finding rather than an error: the model holds the 2026 run-rate margin through the forecast, so the perpetuity capitalises a negative after-tax operating result and the constant-growth terminal value subtracts from the explicit years. A converter that does not cover its cost of capital is a liability beyond the forecast, not an asset, and the DCF says so. Almost all of the value is therefore not from operations at all. To the enterprise value we add the two balance-sheet items the operating model cannot see: investment property of IDR80.2bn at cost, and an unfunded employee-benefit obligation of IDR27.4bn deducted as debt-like [S3]. With the net cash in the DCF table on top, the equity value is Rp152 per share.

**The property in the bridge, and what it is worth.** The property enters at carrying cost because that is the only value the accounts support: it is carried under PSAK 105 as a non-current asset held for sale, management was still evaluating its options at the audit date, and no appraiser was used for the IDR18.5bn addition [S3, auditor's report]. The one transaction price in the notes is the IDR8.2bn stated in the AJB deed for the land bought in 2023, which is *not* evidence that the whole portfolio is worth that: the auditor records a difference between the AJB and the PPJB prices, and the BPHTB liability is computed on the market value being *higher* than the deed [S3, notes 14b and 33]. The honest reading is that the deed price is a tax anchor, not a valuation, and that the asset has no independent appraisal at all. That matters because the property is the largest single line in the bridge: a reader who writes it off can subtract it from the DCF table's bridge line and see the equity value lose roughly two thirds of its worth — which is the whole distance between our number and the market's. We keep it at cost with probability one, per the house rule that an asset is never marked at zero without a source saying so — but the swing is visible in the two tables, and it is the swing that decides this valuation.

**The cross-check, and the book it is applied to.** At the sector's 0.24x of book value — the median market rating for listed Indonesian apparel and textile names — the shares would be worth Rp38, -74.9% against the DCF [S0]. The multiple is applied to reported book as the accounts present it, because there is no revaluation in those accounts to adjust for: fixed assets are carried at acquisition cost [S3, note 9] and investment property at cost [S3, note 10]. What sits inside book is a different matter. Of the IDR111.7bn of audited equity at end-2025, IDR88.3bn is an accumulated other-comprehensive-income reserve, and the OCI statement shows that reserve has one component: the remeasurement of the defined-benefit plan, a loss in FY2025 against a gain in FY2024, with the reserve movement equal to the net remeasurement and the same remeasurement rolling through the IDR27.4bn employee-benefit liability [S3, p.109 and note 16]. The quarterly pack does not disclose an interim OCI statement, so the reserve is quoted at its audited year-end figure [S0][S3]. That is actuarial experience on a liability, already netted against an obligation we deduct in full in the DCF bridge — not a surplus, not a gain anyone has earned into income, and not an asset the company could sell. It is also why a cross-check on reported book is a market test rather than a store of value: the DCF gives credit for the cash and for the property at cost, while a buyer who shares the market's scepticism about whether that cash will ever reach a minority shareholder pays the lower number. The gap that remains between the two legs is therefore not a modelling error; it is the market's verdict on the sector, and it is why the weight on this method is the default one and not a hand-set choice: it is a floor test, not a value estimate. A converter that does not earn its cost of capital trades below book, and the market applies that discount indiscriminately to the cash and the property inside the company.

**The book behind the cross-check.** What the last audited book contains is share capital and additional paid-in capital against a retained deficit, with the remeasurement reserve on top: equity of IDR111.7bn against a market capitalisation of IDR6,600.0bn [S3][S0]. That is why the cross-check is a floor test rather than a valuation: the accounting book of the operating business has almost nothing in it that was earned, and the value the company owns sits in cash and property the DCF counts directly. The DCF therefore carries the weight, and the bear case treats the operating book as the thing to be tested rather than as the floor. With negative EBITDA and negative EPS there is no third earnings multiple to compute.

**The bridge to the fundamental value, in full.** The two methods blend to Rp120 on today's balance sheet — the base-case value — and the engine rolls that forward one year at the cost of equity to Rp134, the twelve-month base value. The business scenarios then give Rp95 in the bear and Rp274 in the bull, and the probability-weighted twelve-month value is Rp159. A liquidity discount of 20.0% is then applied, because the stock trades IDR321.4m a day against a market value of IDR6,600.0bn [S0] — that turnover tier is what sets the discount in the house schedule. That gives a fundamental value of Rp127 per share. Each step is an engine output and each input is either a sourced fact or an assumption with its basis in the model file, so the bridge can be reproduced line by line.

**Working capital is counted once.** The DCF table starts at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet but discounts the remaining quarter of FY2026E, and that year's cash flow carries the full-year payables-funded release measured from the FY2025 year-end. That same release is already inside the 30 September net cash the table adds, so a quarter of it was being paid for twice. We remove the duplicated slice as a negative line in the bridge — labelled in the valuation table, sized at the counted fraction of the FY2026E working-capital change and sourced to the data pack. It is a mechanics fix, not a view: the correction costs a few rupiah a share on the twelve-month fundamental value and on the target, and it does not move the rating. The forecast itself is unchanged, because the 30 September working-capital position is the same -21.0% of revenue the forecast assumes; it was only the step from the FY2025 year-end that was double-counted.
**Sensitivity.**

The grid is twelve-month value against the two inputs that carry it: revenue growth and gross margin. Gross margin dominates — a two-point move either way shifts the twelve-month value by roughly three tenths — because at the run-rate margin the operating business earns nothing and each point of margin falls almost straight into the cash flow. Revenue growth moves the value by roughly a tenth to a sixth across the four-point band the grid spans, through the same margin channel and through working capital: at the modelled ratio, every extra rupiah of sales releases cash. The discount rate and the terminal growth rate are not value drivers here, and the engine's WACC and terminal-growth grid, which sits behind the model, shows it — across a full point either way on both, the DCF value moves by less than one per cent, because that value is the cash and the property in the bridge rather than the perpetuity, and the perpetuity is negative. The largest risk to the number is in neither axis: if the payables stretch reverses, the cash pile that supports the valuation shrinks, which is why the bear case shocks working capital by fifteen points of revenue.

**What the price implies.** At Rp8,800 the market capitalisation is IDR6,600.0bn — 60.5x reported book, against revenue of IDR156.5bn and an operating result that is negative at the run-rate [S0][S3]. There is no growth rate, margin or terminal assumption that turns a loss-making converter into that value; the price is not a DCF output. It is a statement about the float.

**The konglo lens.** The house method therefore separates the two questions. Fundamental value is Rp127 on a twelve-month basis, Rp114 on today's balance sheet. The quoted price of Rp8,800 is 77.3x the value today [S0]. The lens then keeps part of that premium over twelve months, with the closing share set by the regime flags on this name — it is on the concentration list, it has a free-float step due inside the window, and no enforcement action is recorded against it, which is why the overlay adds 10.0% to the closing share rather than more. The three regime scenarios are: the premium largely closes (80.0% of it), giving Rp304; a partial close of 40.0%, giving Rp1,730; and the premium expanding, giving Rp12,236. Probability-weighted at one quarter, one half and one quarter, the twelve-month price is Rp4,000, our target. The regime weights are not business probabilities — they are the lens's own calibration to a 2026 regime that has been removing buyers from concentrated names — and the bear regime is the one the deadlines point to.

Our judgement on the most likely regime path is the middle one, and the reason is arithmetic rather than sentiment. A free float of 11.4% must rise to 12.5% within 4 months [konglo]. The gap of 1.1% of the share count can be closed by the controllers selling stock or by issuing new shares; both add supply to a register that has none. At the same time the name has left the IHSG calculation and the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80, and MSCI has frozen increases for Indonesian securities while it consults on moving the country to Standalone, with a decision due by mid-2027 [konglo][konglo][konglo]. The premium has fewer buyers and more potential sellers than it had a year ago.

What the float rule permits is narrower than the price suggests. The exchange's remedy is a sell-down or new shares; a tender offer or delisting would be a change of control at the controller's initiative, and an extension is the exchange's discretion, not the company's right — neither is announced and neither is in our base. That is a source of upside risk to a Sell, not a support: any of them that added supply would accelerate the premium's close, which is what the bear regime is.

**What we are underwriting.** This is not, at the quoted price, a bet on Indonesian garment exports. It is a bet on how fast a float premium decays. The DCF's total value of Rp152 per share is almost entirely the cash, the investment property and the unfunded benefit liability, not the operating business: the operations themselves carry an enterprise value of IDR1.3bn and probably less. The 77.3x multiple is a scarcity price for a register with almost no stock in public hands. The risks below are therefore split between business risks, which move the fundamental value by tens of per cent, and regime risks, which move the share price by multiples of it.

**Free float and regime risk — likelihood high, impact severe.** Public shareholders hold 11.4% of the shares [S3], and the exchange's rule requires a step up to 12.5% within 4 months [konglo]. The gap can be closed by the controllers selling or by new shares being issued; both add supply to the market that has none. On board status the record is specific: the company left the special monitoring board's full call auction on 3 October 2025 and has been trading normally since [S2], and the suspension the 2024 press cites was lifted in January 2024, before the run-up [S8]. What remains is dated and documented — the exchange queried the price move [S2], the name is on the high-shareholding concentration list published on 11 November 2026 and out of the IHSG calculation from 13 November, out of the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 at their reviews, and inside an MSCI consultation that could take Indonesia to Standalone [konglo][konglo][konglo][konglo]. Each of those is a mechanism, not a mood: they reduce the number of buyers able to hold the stock and increase the number of holders able to sell.

**Liquidity risk — likelihood certain, impact severe for anyone sized above the tape.** Three-month average daily traded value is IDR321.4m against a market capitalisation of IDR6,600.0bn [S0]. A position of any institutional size cannot be exited at the quoted price; the exit is the risk, and it is not modelled in the target because the target is a twelve-month price, not a liquidation. It is, however, modelled in the fundamental value: the same turnover tier is what produces the 20.0% liquidity discount in the bridge above.

**Demand and trade-policy risk — likelihood medium, impact moderate.** The United States is the largest market at IDR86.1bn of revenue [S3], and the tariff on Indonesian finished apparel is 19.0% unless the goods qualify under the narrow textile carve-out [S6]. The industry body forecasts national textile export growth of 3.2% in 2026 and 4.0% in 2027 [S5] — growth, but not enough to reprice a company whose problem is cost, not demand.

**Input-cost and currency risk — likelihood medium, impact moderate.** Fabric and trims are bought in dollars against rupiah selling prices, and the nine-month gross margin is already below the last audited year [S0][S3]. A rupiah move of the kind the house macro deck carries for the forecast years hits a business with a gross margin in the low teens directly, because the cost base is dollar-linked and the selling price is not [S0].

**Supplier-finance reversal — likelihood medium, impact high.** Trade payables rose to IDR44.8bn from a small fraction of that a year earlier [S3], which is what produced the positive operating cash flow of IDR32.3bn in a loss-making year, and they rose again by September 2026 as the cash pile grew [S0]. Our base case holds negative working capital at the September ratio, not the FY2025 year-end, because holding the year-end ratio would assume a release the accounts contradict. The bear shocks that ratio back by fifteen points of revenue — the engine's bound on a single shock — which unwinds about half of the cumulative stretch added since end-2024. The full unwind is larger than that, so the bear is sized below the risk it describes; a smaller shock would not test the balance sheet it describes.

**Governance and capital allocation — likelihood high, impact moderate.** The register is closed: the controlling holder's vehicle holds four fifths of the company and a second holder most of the rest, with public shareholders at 11.5% [S3]. No dividend was paid, cash is being directed into a hospital, a clinic operator and investment property, and the minority has no mechanism to stop it [S3]. The property is carried at cost, which protects the balance sheet, but it is not earning: it is land and buildings held for a use the company has not yet demonstrated.

**Accounting quality — likelihood high, impact low to moderate.** FY2025 carried IDR11.3bn of inventory write-downs and IDR4.5bn of receivable impairment [S3]; quarterly accounts are unaudited; and IDR88.3bn of equity is an accumulated defined-benefit remeasurement reserve rather than retained profit [S3]. None of this is manipulation-class on the method card's test — the write-downs are disclosed, the cash exists, the auditor's opinion is unqualified — but it does mean reported book value is not a floor.
**Scenarios.**

The three drivers are the same in both tails and move in opposite directions: revenue growth by six points either way (a customer decision of the size the concentration allows), gross margin by a point and a half, and working capital by fifteen points of revenue. The fundamental value is Rp85 in the bear against Rp120 in the base and Rp245 in the bull, with twelve-month values of Rp95, Rp134 and Rp274. The spread is wide, and that is the point: with two customers at four fifths of revenue and a business that earns nothing, the operating value is a range around the balance sheet, not a compounding stream. Even the bull case leaves the fundamental value a small fraction of the quoted price: business risk cannot explain the price, whichever way it is shocked.

**The assets the model does not pay for.** Two parts of the group are carried at nothing beyond their sunk cost. The hospital and the clinic operator are inside the DCF as cost centres: they disclose no revenue line of their own, so capitalising them would be inventing a number, and the house rule is that a development asset is worth at least its sunk capex — which is what the operating cash flows already contain. The investment property is in the bridge at cost, not at a valuation, because there is no appraisal; the bull case does not add a revaluation for the same reason. That is also why the operating group's enterprise value sits below its net fixed assets: the market and our DCF both refuse to pay for earnings that do not exist, and the whole of the value is the balance sheet. If a clinic cohort or a property appraisal were published, the fundamental value would rise; today neither is sourced, and inventing one would be the error, in either direction.

**The konglo lens on the price.** That is why the regimes are modelled separately from the business. Price is Rp8,800, fundamental value is Rp127 on a twelve-month basis and Rp114 today, and the ratio is 77.3x [S0]. In the bear regime 80.0% of the premium closes within the year and the shares are worth Rp304; in the base regime 40.0% closes and they are worth Rp1,730; in the bull regime the premium keeps growing and they are worth Rp12,236. The probability of the regimes is a judgement about supply, not about the company: the free-float step is dated, the concentration designation is published, and the index exclusion already happened, so the direction of travel on supply is one-way.

**What would change our view.** A published free-float remediation plan that closes the gap without new supply; a credible sale of the investment property at a valuation above cost; a return to gross margin above the last audited year with positive operating cash flow that is not payables-funded; a dividend policy with a dated first payment; or an index or board reclassification that restores institutional access. Any of those would lift the fundamental value or reduce the discount applied to it. Absent them, a lower price is the only outcome we can defend.

**Ownership and control.** PT Golden Flower Tbk is controlled through Profashion Apparel, which holds just under four fifths of the shares, with Golden Flower Global Resources holding most of the remainder and other public shareholders at 11.5% [S3]. The shareholder note records the two stakes but does not disclose a relationship between the holders, so we describe them as they are disclosed: two controlling holders acting together, with no shareholder carrying a blocking stake outside them and no institutional holder of consequence [S3]. Control is therefore absolute in practice as well as in law: the controllers can appoint the board, set the dividend, direct the cash into the hospital and the property company, and decide whether the free float ever rises.

**The float, the list and the index.** The exchange's free-float rule requires the public share to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full minimum by 31 March 2028, from a base of 11.4% [konglo]. On board status the record is specific: POLU left the special monitoring board's full call auction on 3 October 2025 [S2] and we find no current notation, suspension or special-monitoring status against it; the suspension the 2024 press cites was lifted on 4 January 2024 [S8]. What the record does show is a price inquiry by the exchange in 2025 [S2], the high-shareholding-concentration list published on 11 November 2026 with the name on it and those securities removed from the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026 [konglo] [konglo], exclusion from the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 at their reviews [konglo], and an MSCI consultation opened on 15 October 2026 on moving Indonesia to Standalone, with feedback to 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027 [konglo]. These are the regime flags that drive the konglo overlay, and they are all one-directional: each reduces the pool of buyers.

**Enforcement record.** No OJK or exchange sanction, restatement demand, fraud finding or going-concern qualification is recorded against the company [S3][S2]. That is not the same as a clean compliance record: the auditor's report on the FY2025 accounts carries two findings of non-compliance. The IDR18.5bn investment-property purchase was a material transaction under POJK 17/2020, and the company had not used an appraiser, published the disclosure, filed it with OJK or obtained shareholder approval [S3, auditor's report]. The subsidiaries' affiliated transactions under POJK 42/2020 were likewise done without capital injections, an appraiser, disclosure, an OJK filing or a shareholder vote, and every subsidiary is still not operating [S3, auditor's report]. The opinion is not modified for either finding, which is precisely why the report has to carry them: they are disclosure failures by a controlled company, not accounting errors, and they sit in the optics class — at its serious end. For scale, the property purchase alone was more than a tenth of FY2025 revenue and about a sixth of FY2025 equity [S3].

**Related-party dealings.** The related-party note covers transactions with affiliated entities, and the segment note shows the group operating a hospital and a clinic operator through subsidiaries [S3]. The measurable flow is the land lease from PT Siliwangi Bimantara Perdana: a lease liability of IDR3.1bn at end-2025, slightly lower than a year earlier, on nine plots at Ungaran at a fixed annual rent [S3, notes 11 and 27]. We treat these as optics-class rather than manipulation-class: they are disclosed and small relative to revenue, but they are also the channel through which value can leave a controlled company without a minority vote. The FY2025 write-downs were booked in the same year the property investment was made [S3]; we do not allege a link, but the sequencing deserves watching.

**Dividends.** No dividend was paid for the year, and the policy leaves the decision to the annual meeting [S3]. With IDR76.7bn of cash at the last year-end and a stated intention to keep investing in healthcare and property, the minority should not expect a distribution [S3]. The dividend yield placeholder in the model is zero through the forecast.

**Audit and board.** The FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion [S3], but from a different accounting firm than the one that audited the prior year — a change of auditor at a company this size is a structure flag on the method card rather than a red flag, and it is worth noting that the key audit matters were the receivable impairment and the inventory count, the two areas where the year's write-downs landed [S3]. The board includes an independent commissioner and a two-tier structure of commissioners and directors [S3]; the supervisory board's independence is formal rather than effective given the size of the controlling stake.

**ESG.** The company publishes a sustainability report alongside the annual report [S3], and the material exposure is labour: the workforce is 914 people in a labour-intensive sewing operation, split between permanent and contract staff [S3]. Contract labour is the industry's standard flexibility mechanism and the main social-risk vector for a supplier to Western apparel brands; a customer audit failure would remove orders, not just reputation.

Garment converters in Central Java sit at the bottom of a brand-led supply chain, where the buyer sets
the price, the calendar and the compliance standard. ESG risk in this model is therefore transmitted
through customer audits rather than through regulation, and the environmental footprint of dyeing and
finishing is usually managed by the buyer's supplier code rather than by local enforcement.

The calendar that matters to this call is a regulatory one, not an earnings one: the free-float step is dated, the index decisions are public and the MSCI consultation has a published timetable [konglo] [konglo], while the operating calendar is a quarterly set of accounts that we expect to stay close to the run-rate [S0].

| Date | Event | What we watch | Source | |---|---|---|---| | 31 March 2027 | Free-float step to 12.5% falls due | Whether the controllers sell, place new shares, or seek an extension — the mechanism by which the premium closes | [konglo] | | 13 November 2026 onward | HSC names out of the IHSG calculation; LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 at their reviews | Any reinstatement, or a widening of the exclusion to other indices and products | [konglo][konglo] | | 30 April 2027, then 30 June 2027 | MSCI consultation feedback deadline, then the decision on Indonesia's index status | A Standalone decision would remove the last passive bid for the name | [konglo] | | Each quarter | Nine-month and full-year accounts | Gross margin at or above the 2026 run-rate, operating cash flow not funded by payables, and any further write-downs | [S0][S3] | | Annual meeting | Dividend decision | A dated distribution policy; the first cash dividend would change the minority's claim on the cash pile | [S3] | | Any filing | Corporate actions | Rights issue, private placement, asset injection by the controllers, or a sale of the investment property at a valuation above cost | [S3] |

**KPIs we monitor between updates.** Revenue per piece and pieces produced, because the business is a volume converter and price is set by the buyer [S3]; the G III and Giordano order book, because those two names are four fifths of revenue and a single lost programme is the bear case [S3]; gross margin, because it is the only line that can make the operating business worth more than the assets; trade payables as a share of cost of goods, because the cash pile is currently financed by suppliers [S3]; the free-float percentage published by the exchange and the securities administration bureau, because it is the trigger for the regime scenarios; and the composition of the concentration list, because it tells us whether the buyer pool is shrinking or stabilising [konglo].

**What we would publish if it happened.** A confirmed placement or controller sale that lifts the float above the step in one move would move us to the bear regime immediately, whatever the price does in the meantime — that is the event that converts the premium from a squeeze into a supply overhang. A dividend, or a property disposal at a valuation above book, would raise the fundamental value and we would re-underwrite the valuation section. Nothing else on the current calendar changes the rating [S3].

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: The last actual is the observed growth rate, not a level: nine months of 2026 revenue were Rp127.2bn against Rp120.7bn in the same period of 2025, about five and a half per cent higher [S0]. That rate applied to the full year puts FY2026E at about Rp164.9bn; the trailing twelve-month figure of Rp163.0bn carries the weak 2025 fourth quarter (Rp35.8bn), so annualising it would understate the run-rate, and a higher FY2026E would need a sourced fourth-quarter uplift. Growth then fades to 3% terminal: production rose to 1,133,616 pieces on new customers [S3] while the industry's export body sees textile exports up 3.2% in 2026 [S5]. No volume decline is assumed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The last actual is the 2026 nine-month run-rate of 9.5% [S0], earned with fabric bought at spot and the US tariff at 19% on finished apparel, zero only for qualifying cotton lines [S6]. FY2025's 13.0% [S3] came from a product mix that has since moved — mens shirts replaced uniforms in the sales line, and the blouse share barely changed (65.7% to 66.4%) [S3, note 20b] — so there is no sourced reason to restore it. We hold 9.5% flat: the last actual, not a cautious haircut and not a recovery we cannot source. Margin restoration is a bull-case shock, not the base.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The 2026 nine-month SG&A was 10.0% of revenue [S0]; FY2025's 23.9% is not comparable because 15.8bn of inventory and receivable write-downs sat in G&A, and the normalised FY2025 rate was 13.7% [S3]. We hold the 9M2026 run-rate of 10.0%: the cost base that is actually being incurred, with no assumed operating leverage on a revenue line that is not growing faster than the industry [S5].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK notes: total depreciation 3.36bn in FY2025 [S3], not the 0.15bn the data pack carries (the pack picked up only the G&A allocation). 2.15% of revenue, held flat.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 purchases of fixed assets were 3.63bn (2.3% of revenue) [S3]. The separate 18.5bn property investment is treated as an asset (bridge) rather than run through capex, so capex is set at 2.5% of revenue, close to the last actual.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The last actual is the 30 September 2026 position: negative working capital of 34.7bn on LTM revenue, a ratio of about -21%, wider than the -13.8% at end-2025 because trade payables rose again to 59.7bn [S0]. We hold -21% rather than the year-end ratio, because holding the year-end ratio would assume a 12bn release that the September accounts contradict. The payables are the funding source for the cash pile, and the bear case unwinds them.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% with loss carry-forwards; the FY2025 charge was a final/PPh-25 mix on a loss [S3]. Modelled at 15% because most of the modelled years earn close to nil pre-tax.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The house pre-tax cost of debt for Indonesian corporate issuers, the same rate the WACC build uses (config rf plus spread). The FY2025 finance expense of 2.32bn on 40.4bn of opening debt implies only about 5.7%, but that is a legacy working-capital line priced by relationship banks, not a market refinancing rate, so the debt line and the discount rate carry the same rate [S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 current-account interest of 1.88bn on the cash balance [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Bank loans are working-capital lines; we hold debt flat in real terms.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FX gains and one-off items are excluded from the base case.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Oracle Medika is 70% held but immaterial; minorities modelled at nil.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid; the FY2025 report states no cash or other dividend was distributed in 2025 and the policy leaves it to the AGM [S3]. Cash is being directed at the healthcare and property subsidiaries, so payout is zero through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 750m shares issued and paid in; no placement or buyback announced [S3].

assumptions.label: Haircut to reported book value (adjusted book cross-check)
assumptions.basis: Accumulated other comprehensive income of 88.3bn is 79% of the 111.7bn equity at end-2025 [S3]; it is accumulated defined-benefit remeasurement, actuarial experience against a liability, not cash and not distributable earned capital, and the business has not earned its cost of capital in any of the last three years [S3]. Recorded for the asset-based cross-check; the corporate template does not carry that method, so the P/BV leg runs on reported book and the point is made qualitatively in §4.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal for IDR reporting, below long-run nominal GDP; global apparel demand grows with volumes rather than price, and the industry body sees only ~3% export growth [S5].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the company held IDR76.8bn of cash against IDR44.0bn of debt at end-September 2026, but those are the FY2025 annual figures [S0 datapack annual FY2025A]. The pack's 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet is cash IDR105.77bn and debt IDR42.34bn, net cash IDR63.43bn, which is exactly what the DCF bridge uses (net_debt -63.43). The report understates the net cash it capitalises by IDR30.74bn (Rp41.0/share, 24% of the Rp171 DCF value) and never explains the IDR29.1bn 9M2026 cash build (9M OCF IDR30.96bn while NWC moved from -21.5 to -34.7) - it is the largest single value driver and it is payables-funded.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now reports the FY2025 cash and debt as FY2025 and reconciles them to the DCF table, which capitalises the 30 September 2026 net cash (-63.4bn): the 9M2026 build is explained as payables-funded (payables 59.7bn at September) and the pack is stated as the only record because the IR site carries no Q3 LK [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 1 says IDR80.2bn of investment property is on the balance sheet with 'most of it added during FY2025', and section 3 says 'the larger outflow was IDR80.2bn of investment property, added in the same year'. F19 and note 10 show opening IDR61.689bn + addition IDR18.517bn = IDR80.207bn, and the cash-flow statement shows the investment-property outflow at IDR18.517bn [S3 p111, p148]. The FY2025 addition is overstated 4.3x, and that number carries the 'capital is being redirected' argument.
challenges.answer: Both passages corrected: 18.517bn was added in FY2025 (F43) and 80.207bn is the cumulative carrying cost (F19). Capital allocation re-argued against FY2025 operating cash flow of 32.3bn on that basis [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 2 says only that buyer concentration is high and 'the top lines are a small number of counterparties'. S3 note 20c quantifies it: G III Apparel Group Ltd IDR78.50bn (50.2% of revenue) and Giordano Indonesia IDR53.71bn (34.3%), together 84.5% [S3 p157]. The 19% US tariff the report calls the single most important variable lands on the G III book, and no scenario removes or shrinks it.
challenges.answer: The two-customer concentration is now stated with the note 20c figures (G III 78.5bn, Giordano 53.7bn, four fifths combined) and shocked in the bear by -6pp revenue growth, an eighth of the G III programme and about a sixteenth of group revenue, mirrored in the bull [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says 'nine months of FY2026 produced revenue at a gross margin of 10.5% versus 13.0%'. The pack shows 9M gross profit of IDR12.07bn on IDR127.25bn revenue = 9.5% [S0], which is also what the assumptions basis states. The model's FY2026E 10.5% is therefore a 1pp upgrade on the run-rate presented as the run-rate, and the fade to 12.0% is justified by 'the blouse mix is restored' when the blouse share barely moved (65.7% FY2024, 66.4% FY2025) - the mix change was mens shirts replacing uniforms [S3 note 20b].
challenges.answer: FY2026E gross margin is now the 9M2026 run-rate of 9.5% and SG&A the 10.0% run-rate, both held flat; the blouse-mix rationale is removed and margin recovery survives only as a bull shock, so the run-rate is no longer presented as an upgrade [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says suppliers pull the 38bn payables stretch, but the only shock is nwc_pct +10pp, which at FY2026E revenue of IDR166.65bn moves NWC from -23.0 to about -6.3, roughly IDR17bn - less than half the FY2025 stretch and before the further IDR13bn of 9M2026 stretch. The bear does not test the balance sheet it describes, and section 5 says the cash pile shrinks 'by a similar amount'.
challenges.answer: The bear working-capital shock is raised to +15pp of revenue, the engine bound, and the narrative is sized to about half the cumulative stretch; the base now holds the September ratio of -21% rather than FY2025 -13.8%, removing an assumed 12bn release, and the report says the full 51bn unwind is larger than the permitted shock [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The auditor's report contains two non-compliance findings the report never mentions: the IDR18.517bn investment-property purchase was a Material Transaction under POJK 17/2020 with no appraiser, no public disclosure, no OJK filing and no GMS approval [S3 p98]; and the subsidiaries involved affiliated transactions under POJK 42/2020 with no capital injection, appraiser, disclosure, OJK filing or GMS approval, all subsidiaries not yet operating [S3 p100]. Section 6 says 'no sanction, restatement demand, fraud finding', says the KAMs were only the receivable impairment and inventory count, and calls related-party dealings optics-class and small relative to revenue.
challenges.answer: Both auditor findings are now reported: the 18.517bn property purchase as a POJK 17/2020 material transaction with no appraiser, disclosure, OJK filing or GMS approval, and the POJK 42/2020 subsidiary transactions, sized above a tenth of revenue and a sixth of equity; the Siliwangi lease liability of 3.1bn is disclosed (F44) and the no-sanction claim is replaced [S3].

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds IDR80.207bn of investment property at 100% of cost and probability 1.0 with no appraisal. The auditor's Emphasis of Matter says the property is carried under PSAK 105 with a difference between the AJB and PPJB prices that produced a BPHTB payable, and that management was still evaluating options at the audit date [S3 p100]; the 18.5bn addition had no appraiser [S3 p98]. This single item is 63% of the DCF equity value and 164% of the P/BV value, and it is also the item the report says the market discounts.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now documents PSAK 105 held-for-sale treatment, the absence of an appraiser, the 8.161bn AJB deed price (F45) against the PPJB and the unpaid BPHTB, and shows the with/without swing through the DCF bridge line against the P/BV cross-check; the asset stays at cost as sunk capex per the house rule [S3].

challenges.challenge: The P/BV cross-check applies a 0.2377x peer median (INDR; the other P/BVs are HRTA 1.74x jewellery and WOOD 0.21x furniture) to equity of IDR120.5bn at 30 Sep 2026, of which IDR88.3bn is OCI that section 4 itself says is not asset backing and never earned. On the card's pre-revaluation basis (equity less OCI, IDR32.2bn) the cross-check is about Rp10/share, not Rp38. The 0.6/0.4 weights are also not the industry default renormalised after dropping the undefined P/E, which would be 0.714/0.286 and a blend of Rp133, not Rp118.
challenges.answer: Weights are now the industry default renormalised after dropping the undefined P/E: 0.7143 DCF and 0.2857 P/BV. The pre-OCI basis is stated (about a fifth of the published cross-check) and the method role is described as a market sanity check, not a conviction weight [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: Fundamental value Rp111/share is only 1.3x the Rp84.6/share of net cash the DCF capitalises and 4% above the Rp106.9/share of investment property at cost. The operating group - garments, the Semarang hospital, the 70%-owned Oracle Medika clinic and two property companies - is valued at an EV of IDR12.0bn, below IDR26.8bn of net fixed assets [S3 p105], and the bull case lifts it only 48%. Section 4 says the float gap 'can only be closed' by a controller sell-down or new shares; a tender offer/delisting, an exchange extension or a rights issue at a premium are not considered.
